newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korean soldier spoils Gingrich border tour.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean soldier spoils Gingrich border tour.

text.p: A security scare forced U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich to change plans during a tour of the heavily fortified border dividing North and South Korea on Tuesday.
Gingrich, heading a 12-member congressional delegation to South Korea, had been scheduled to stop for a briefing at the Bridge of No Return within the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ).
But about 15 minutes before he was due to arrive at the historic site, one of the last relics of the Cold War, a North Korean soldier carrying an AK-47 rifle was spotted in the area.
Under the terms of the armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War and established the DMZ, only side arms are allowed inside the so-called Joint Security Area.
"Bringing long arms is prohibited. It is unauthorised to be there and it presents an unusual risk," U.S. military spokesman Jim Coles told reporters.
Gingrich, dressed in a comouflage overcoat, drove by the bridge in a van but did not stop for the scheduled briefing.
The Bridge of No Return spans the border line with two observations posts on either end. Some 20 South Korean and U.S. soldiers guarded the southern post on Tuesday.
At the southern entrance to the 100 metre (109 yard) long concrete bridge a rusted metal sign reads: "Military Demarcation Line. Do Not Enter."
Earlier, Gingrich peered through binoculars at an observation point overlooking a North Korean village built as a model settlement in a propaganda war with the South.
"This is a great opportunity for us to reinforce, for anyone who has any doubts at all, that we are committed to defend Korea," he told reporters.
The United States helps guard the border with 37,000 troops.
Gingrich described the DMZ as a great success story, adding: "For 44 years it's worked and I hope it works until unification".
Last April, North Korea sparked a security alert by repeatedly sending dozens of troops carrying heavy weapons into the Joint Security Area.
This followed an announcement by Pyongyang that it would no longer abide by the terms of the armistice.
Gingrich and his team arrived on Monday for a three-day visit, the first stop of an Asian tour that will also take them to China, Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan.
In South Korea, they discussed issues ranging from proposed peace talks with North Korea to trade in meetings with senior officials, including President Kim Young-sam.

Representative Jay Kim of California, the first ethnic Korean elected to Congress, told reporters a bill he proposed to allow visa-free travel for South Koreans to the United States would pass sometime this year.
Seoul has been pressing hard for easier travel to smooth trade and tourism.
Jay Kim also said congress would put pressure on Taiwan to reverse its controversial plans to ship low-grade nuclear waste to North Korea.
